opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, what surprised me most wasn't that it worked. We had reasons to believe that scaling the context would work if we got the engineering and the modeling right. The surprise was how quickly people found uses we hadn't really anticipated.

When we were pushing toward very long contexts, the mental model internally was fairly simple: you can put a whole book in, or a long document, and ask questions about it. That's useful, but it's a bit of a "bigger retrieval" framing. What people actually did was more creative. They dropped in entire codebases and asked the model to reason across files, find bugs, or explain how a system fits together. That's very different from looking something up. It's closer to having a colleague who has read everything at once and can hold it in their head.

Video was another one. Once you can fit an hour or more of video into context, you can ask about something that happened at minute forty-three, or how two moments relate. The model isn't just transcribing. It's connecting things across a long span of time, and that opens up a whole set of applications we hadn't fully thought through.

The thing I find most interesting scientifically is in-context learning at that scale. If you give the model a large amount of material about something it has never really seen, like documentation for an obscure tool or reference material for a low-resource language, it can pick up a surprising amount of that skill just from context, without any fine-tuning. That blurs the line between what the model knows from training and what it can learn on the fly. I think that's a deep direction, because it suggests part of the future isn't just bigger pretraining but models that adapt in the moment to whatever you hand them.

There are still open problems. Cost and latency matter a lot when you're processing millions of tokens. And "can technically attend to everything" isn't the same as "reasons perfectly over everything." Finding a needle is one thing; synthesizing across many needles is harder. But overall, the gap between what we built it for and what people did with it was the most delightful part.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the thing that surprised me most is honestly how much it just worked once we pushed on it. Going into the 1.5 effort, there was a reasonable prior in the field that attention would degrade badly as you stretched context, that models would get lost in the middle, that you'd need some fundamentally different architecture. And what we found is that when you actually train for it and do the engineering carefully, the model can go to a million tokens, even ten million in our internal experiments, and still do needle-in-a-haystack retrieval essentially perfectly. That was a genuinely nice moment. We'd been so used to context being this scarce resource that you had to ration.

The second surprise is more about what people do with it. My mental model was "okay, you can put in a long document and ask questions." And people do that, obviously. But the more interesting uses are the ones where you're putting in a whole modality of information that previously didn't fit anywhere. Someone drops in an hour of video and asks where a specific thing happened. Someone puts in an entire codebase and asks it to find the bug across files, not just within a function. One that stuck with me was the Kalamang experiment, where you put a grammar book and a dictionary for a language with almost no speakers into the context, and the model learns to translate it at a level comparable to a human who studied the same materials. That's not retrieval. That's learning something new, in context, at inference time. And to me that's the conceptually big thing. For a long time the only way to teach a model something was gradient descent. Now there's this second path where you just show it, and the amount you can show it has grown by orders of magnitude.

The third thing, which is less flashy, is how it changes how people think about building. A lot of the RAG scaffolding that developers were putting together was really a workaround for small context. When you don't need to chunk and embed and hope you retrieved the right piece, a lot of complexity just disappears. Now, I don't think long context replaces retrieval entirely. If you have terabytes of data you still need to narrow it down. But the boundary moved a lot, and I think people are still recalibrating what they can just put in front of the model.

If I'm honest about what's still hard, it's cost and latency. Processing a million tokens isn't free, and the research on making that efficient, with caching and better attention mechanisms, is very active. And the capability isn't uniform. Retrieving one fact is easy. Reasoning over many pieces of information scattered across the whole context, synthesizing them, that's where there's still real headroom. So I'd say I'm surprised by how far we got, and also pretty clear that we're early in understanding what people will do once it's cheap and fast.

astra-6.text:
What’s surprised me is how much changes when you can put the whole problem in context. Instead of selecting a few passages or trying to summarize everything beforehand, you can give the model a large amount of material and ask questions across it.

And the interesting uses aren’t just about finding one fact in a long document. It’s connecting things that are far apart: understanding how different parts of a codebase relate, or asking a question about a long video that requires information from several moments. That’s a much richer capability than simply having a bigger input window.

I think we’re still discovering what the right interactions look like. People are used to working around limited context, so it takes a little time to ask, “What would I do differently if I could give the model all the relevant information?” That’s where a lot of the interesting experimentation comes from.

sol-6.1.text:
What surprised me is how quickly people found uses that we hadn’t really anticipated. You think of long context as, okay, I can put a very long document into the model and ask questions about it. But people start putting in entire codebases, or video, or a lot of examples of a task, and the interaction becomes quite different.

One thing I find particularly interesting is learning from the context. Instead of training a model specifically for something, you can show it the information it needs, give it examples, and then ask it to do the task. The context starts to feel like a way of programming the model.

And there’s a difference between having a large context window and actually using it well. Finding one fact somewhere in a long input is useful, but connecting things that are far apart, across different modalities, is much more exciting. I think we’re still discovering what people will do when they can bring that much information into a single conversation.
